intro: The second part moves from a slow night scene through the choosing of a sacrificial victim to her final dance. This composer-conducted recording uses Stravinsky’s later, 1943 revision of the “Sacrificial Dance”, not an untouched 1913 performing text.
question: When a short chord keeps returning, do its interruptions become as important as the chord itself?

sections.label: Mystic Circles of the Young Girls

cues.title: A second beginning
cues.text: Part II starts slowly rather than continuing the first part’s final rush. Broad, separated phrases prepare a different ritual: the choosing and sacrifice of one girl from the group.
cues.evidence: The score’s second Introduction begins at rehearsal 79, Largo. The report has low attack activity in its opening windows. The scenario is documented in Van den Toorn, chapter 1.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sound gathers, then recedes
cues.text: The opening paragraph does not simply grow louder. Its sound expands and retreats in successive waves; listen for the quieter space around a phrase as well as the phrase’s fullest point.
cues.evidence: The report rises through 0:20–0:30, falls at 0:35, then rises again at 0:40–0:50. This cue describes measured relative level, not an identified chord.

cues.title: An imagined ancient ceremony
cues.text: Stravinsky and Nicholas Roerich devised the ballet’s scenario together. Its prehistoric sacrifice is a theatrical construction, not a documented reconstruction of a specific ancient Russian ceremony.
cues.evidence: Van den Toorn, chapter 1, pp. 5–11, considers Roerich’s scenario, Stravinsky’s accounts and the absence of a corresponding sacrifice in standard accounts of Russian paganism: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html#d0e414

cues.title: Wait through the quiet
cues.text: This slow introduction repeatedly withholds a firm dance pulse. Instead of imposing a beat on every sound, follow the spacing between gestures and the length of their sustained tails.
cues.evidence: The score’s Largo introduction and the report’s sparse attack activity support a passage-level listening strategy. No instrumental release is timed at 1:55.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A low-level middle stretch
cues.text: The middle of the introduction leaves an extended quieter span. Its eventual growth matters because the music has allowed that lower level to persist; compare the breadth of the change with the abrupt cuts later in the part.
cues.evidence: Relative level stays low around 2:00–2:30 and increases through 2:40–3:00. The report supplies the contour, not a harmonic interpretation.

cues.title: Prepare for a repeated pattern
cues.text: Near the end of the introduction, keep the slow spacing in memory. The next section gives the dancers a recurring figure to circle around; recurrence will replace the opening’s less regular succession of gestures.
cues.evidence: The transition from rehearsals 90 to 91 leads into Mystic Circles. The report’s strong 3:42 boundary locates the approximate change; this cue precedes it without asserting a last bar.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The girls circle
cues.text: “Mystic Circles” turns to recurrent material instead of introducing a continuously developing tune. Listen for small returns and extensions: the choreography’s repeated circling has a musical counterpart, but not a simple one-beat-per-step illustration.
cues.evidence: Rehearsal 91 begins Mystic Circles; the report changes strongly at 3:42. Van den Toorn’s chapters 1 and 7 discuss the relation between the dance scenario and recurring musical blocks.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A phrase fills out
cues.text: The circling passage grows and then quickly withdraws. Compare the fuller statement with the softer material around it: repeated material can change its weight without changing into a completely new section.
cues.evidence: The report rises around 4:20–4:35 and falls sharply by 4:45. This is a measured passage contour, not a claim that an exact theme return begins at 4:30.

cues.title: A remembered vision
cues.text: Stravinsky later described the ballet’s conception as a vision of a girl dancing herself to death before elders. That account is retrospective: sketches and correspondence reveal a collaborative process with Roerich, not an independently witnessed moment of inspiration.
cues.evidence: Van den Toorn, chapter 1, pp. 4–11, compares Stravinsky’s later recollections with the scenario’s documentary history: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html#d0e414

cues.title: The same material, reweighted
cues.text: Follow a recognisable fragment through the later circling music. Its surroundings can become more emphatic even when the fragment itself remains short; listen for what is repeated and what is added around it.
cues.evidence: Van den Toorn, chapter 7, analyses the block construction of Mystic Circles. The report alternates stronger and quieter windows through 5:20–6:10; no motif is machine-identified.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Choosing becomes proclamation
cues.text: The quiet circling gives way to the more forceful “Glorification of the Chosen One”. Reiterated attacks and short, changing groups replace the slower, more continuous motion of the preceding section.
cues.evidence: The score’s Glorification begins at rehearsal 104. The report has major changes at 6:16 and 6:28, with a steep level rise through 6:25–6:30. The 6:28 marker covers the selection/proclamation transition rather than claiming its first stroke.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A forceful sustained span
cues.text: The glorification maintains a much stronger recorded level than the opening night scene. Listen within that sustained force for changing group lengths; loudness alone does not explain the music’s uneven motion.
cues.evidence: The report sustains high relative level and frequent attacks between 6:30 and 8:00. The score supplies the changing rhythmic groupings; the analysis does not measure the notated metre.

cues.title: Keep a pulse underneath
cues.text: Try maintaining a steady small pulse while the larger gestures change length. Losing the expected strong beat is part of the experience; it need not mean that every underlying duration is irregular.
cues.evidence: Van den Toorn, chapters 3–4, distinguishes regular units from irregular grouping in the Rite. This is a strategy for the fast music, not a verified beat grid for the LP transfer.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A short invocation
cues.text: The brief “Evocation of the Ancestors” stands between the glorification and the longer ritual action. Hear it as a concentrated calling gesture, not a new slow movement with an independent development.
cues.evidence: The named sequence is printed in the score and label track list. Cumulative reissue timings suggest about 8:11; the LP report changes around 8:10 and drops into the following section at 8:48. The marker at 8:08 is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The ritual lowers its voice
cues.text: “Ritual Action of the Ancestors” begins from a much quieter level. A recurring accompaniment can hold the ground while longer phrases develop above it; listen for different rates of activity within one texture.
cues.evidence: The score’s Ritual Action begins at rehearsal 121. The report has a boundary at 8:48 and quiet windows from 8:50 onwards. Van den Toorn, chapter 7, discusses its superimposed layers.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A concert life after Paris
cues.text: The ballet’s turbulent first reception did not settle the score’s fate. A Paris concert performance under Pierre Monteux in April 1914 won an enthusiastic response: the work was already acquiring a life without Nijinsky’s original staging.
cues.evidence: Van den Toorn, chapter 1, pp. 2–4, documents the 5 April 1914 Casino de Paris concert and its reception: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html#d0e414

cues.title: A rise out of quiet
cues.text: The ritual’s quiet ground permits a sudden expansion to register strongly. Listen across the approaching rise rather than treating the louder paragraph as an unrelated piece.
cues.evidence: The report moves from low 10:00–10:20 windows to a sharp rise at 10:25–10:30, then recedes at 10:40. The cue precedes the broad measured change.

cues.title: A second, separated crest
cues.text: Another strong wave arrives after the intervening retreat. The ritual builds through separated accumulations, not through one uninterrupted crescendo.
cues.evidence: The report’s second large rise spans 11:00–11:15, separated from the 10:30 crest by a quieter interval. It falls sharply again around 11:25.

cues.title: The space before the dance
cues.text: The later ritual withdraws before the sacrificial dance. Keep listening through the low-level span: the contrast with the next rapid attacks depends on this reduction, not merely on the strength of the attacks themselves.
cues.evidence: Relative level is low from about 11:25 through 12:05, then rises sharply at 12:10–12:20. No exact final sustained note is identified.

cues.title: The final dance begins
cues.text: The “Sacrificial Dance” makes short chord attacks and their separations central. Rather than following a long melody, compare the lengths of successive groups and the interruptions between them.
cues.evidence: The label’s cumulative durations put the final dance near 12:13; the report rises strongly at 12:10–12:20. The 1943 revision retains the dance’s contrasted blocks; no chord spelling from another edition is imposed on the recording.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Force is interrupted
cues.text: The early part of the final dance includes a sharp withdrawal after its initial force. Treat the quieter gap as part of the rhythmic design, not as an accidental loss of momentum.
cues.evidence: High 12:15–12:35 windows give way to much quieter 12:40–12:50 windows. The report establishes the interruption but not the identity of every instrument remaining.

cues.title: Rebuilding in short spans
cues.text: The dance repeatedly rebuilds from quieter material. Follow the return of force across several short spans; no single, evenly paced crescendo governs the whole ending.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises through 13:10–13:35, then drops sharply at 13:40–13:45. The cue describes that broad cycle.

cues.title: A later sacrificial text
cues.text: In 1943 Stravinsky revised the “Sacrificial Dance”, changing notation and scoring. His 1960 recording uses that revision. The composer conducting his own work is therefore not the same thing as preserving every detail of its earliest score.
cues.evidence: The K catalogue identifies the 5–6 January 1960 performance as using the revised Danse sacrale: https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/188-k015-the-rite-of-spring. Van den Toorn, chapter 2, pp. 39–54, explains the separate 1943/1945 text.

cues.title: Remember the recurring block
cues.text: Hold the short attacking idea in memory as the dance continues. Its returns help organise the larger span even when the lengths of intervening passages make an ordinary eight-bar expectation unreliable.
cues.evidence: Van den Toorn, chapters 3–4 and 7, analyses the final dance’s recurring blocks and irregular grouping. This cue does not assert an exact return at 14:55.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Intensity does not run straight
cues.text: Near the end, another strong span is followed by a noticeable retreat. The music reserves space for renewed attacks; listen for the alternation between pressure and release rather than a single continuous ascent.
cues.evidence: The report reaches a strong window at 15:30, falls at 15:40 and grows again through 15:50–16:30. These are relative-level observations only.

cues.title: Hear the final separation
cues.text: The final accumulation ends with separated sounds and their decay. Do not mistake the remaining surface noise of this LP transfer for a sustained orchestral note after the music has stopped.
cues.evidence: The report remains strong through 16:30, drops substantially at 16:35 and reaches a low tail by 16:45; total duration is 16:46.6. No exact final attack time or instrument is claimed.

transitions.title: Slow gestures become a recurring circle
transitions.how: The Largo introduction yields to the recurring material of the girls’ circle. Sustained colour gives way to more clearly patterned movement, but the new section remains restrained. The connection is a change in the organisation of gestures and accompaniment rather than a forceful tonal cadence announcing a new movement.
transitions.evidence: Rehearsals 90–91; the LP report has a strong 3:42 boundary. The label independently places the second section about 3:42 into the part.

transitions.title: Circling is broken by reiterated attacks
transitions.how: The selection of the victim interrupts the circling texture with reiterated, forceful chords. The glorification then organises rapid gestures in changing groups. Instead of gradually increasing the old accompaniment, Stravinsky replaces its scale of motion and orchestral weight. The attacks function as a dividing event between ceremonies.
transitions.evidence: Rehearsals 103–104; major report boundaries at 6:16 and 6:28 and a rising 6:25–6:30 level. The marker covers the transition region, not the first of the selection strokes.

transitions.title: The fast ritual becomes an invocation
transitions.how: The glorification’s sustained rapid activity gives way to the shorter calling gestures of the evocation. Force remains available, but the phrase changes scale: separated orchestral statements replace the preceding stream of short groups. The invocation is a compact link to the longer ritual action that follows.
transitions.evidence: Printed section sequence and Parnassus track durations put the join near 8:11. The LP report changes level and spectral balance around 8:10; 8:08 is a passage marker, not a chord-aligned onset.

transitions.title: A quieter recurring ground takes over
transitions.how: The invocation gives way to a quiet recurring accompaniment. Longer phrases can be laid above that ground without forcing every layer into the same rhythmic cycle. The reduction of orchestral weight establishes room for the ritual’s later expansions; it does not close the work harmonically.
transitions.evidence: Rehearsal 121 and Van den Toorn’s discussion of Ritual Action. The report identifies a boundary at 8:48 followed by low-level 8:50–9:40 windows.

transitions.title: The ritual ground yields to broken chords
transitions.how: The ritual’s final quiet span is replaced by the sharply articulated chords of the sacrificial dance. Their changing group lengths and intervening spaces become the principal source of motion. This recording uses Stravinsky’s 1943 revised text: the structural contrast is clear, but details of its chord voicing must not be borrowed uncritically from the more commonly reprinted finale.
transitions.evidence: The label puts the final dance near 12:13; the report rises sharply across 12:10–12:20 after the quiet 11:25–12:05 span. The K catalogue establishes the 1943 finale used in this performance.

facts: Russia · Switzerland 1914–20 · France 1920–39 · United States from 1939
Sergei Diaghilev · Vaslav Nijinsky · C. F. Ramuz · George Balanchine · W. H. Auden
Ballets, operas, symphonies, sacred choral music and chamber works; three successive approaches to tonality
composer.background:
Igor Stravinsky grew up in a St Petersburg household in which opera was a profession: his father, Fyodor, was a bass at the Mariinsky Theatre. Born at the family’s summer residence in Oranienbaum in 1882, Igor began piano lessons at ten but entered St Petersburg University to study law. Through a fellow student, Vladimir Rimsky-Korsakov, he met Vladimir’s father, whose private teaching became more important than a conservatory course. Regular lessons between 1905 and 1908 covered orchestration as practical work: distributing a passage among instruments, then comparing the result with the teacher’s solution. The Symphony in E♭, Scherzo fantastique and Fireworks belong to this apprenticeship, with traces of Tchaikovsky, Alexander Glazunov and the Russian fairy-tale orchestra.

In 1906 he married his cousin Catherine Nossenko; their four children were born between 1907 and 1914. Sergei Diaghilev heard the young composer’s orchestral music in 1909 and first employed him to orchestrate Chopin for Les Sylphides. A larger commission followed: The Firebird, with choreography by Michel Fokine. Its premiere at the Paris Opéra on 25 June 1910, with Tamara Karsavina in the title role, made Stravinsky’s reputation outside Russia. The distinction between human and supernatural characters is audible in the harmony: folk-like diatonic tunes for Ivan and the princesses, chromatic and symmetrical scales for the Firebird and Kashchei. The closing horn melody expands into an orchestral procession without abandoning its short repeating phrases.
composer.born: 17 June 1882, Oranienbaum, near St Petersburg, Russia
composer.epithet: A composer of ballets who made the placement of an accent as consequential as a change of harmony.
